items.title: Pick a project worth showing
items.description: One real project, finished well, beats five rushed ones. Pick the one that shows how you think.

metadata.youllNeed: Your notes and checkpoints from earlier stages.
metadata.practise: Publish your first case study (Stage 06 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: How to pick a portfolio project that's worth showing
metadata.seoDescription: One finished project beats five rushed ones. Learn how to choose a portfolio project, what makes one worth showing, and how to be honest about it.

quiz.question: What is a portfolio for?
options: Showing that you can think, decide and finish
quiz.why: Quality of thinking matters more than quantity.

quiz.question: Which project is best to show?
options: A pretty one with no story
A copy of a famous app
One with a real problem, a clear role and a process you can explain
quiz.why: You need something you can explain and defend.

quiz.question: Can you combine earlier checkpoints into one case study?
options: Yes, research, flow, wireframes, testing and components can form one story
quiz.why: Those checkpoints already cover most of a project's journey.

quiz.question: What should you do if a project was self-initiated?
options: Claim it was a client job
quiz.why: Honesty builds trust, and it holds up under questions.

items.title: Structure a case study
items.description: A case study is a story with a beginning, a middle and an end: the problem, what you did, and what happened.

metadata.practise: Publish your first case study (Stage 06 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: How to structure a UX case study: a simple skeleton
metadata.seoDescription: A case study is a story, not a gallery of screens. Learn a simple eight-part structure, how to show decisions, and how to keep it easy to skim.

quiz.question: A case study is closest to...
options: A story with a problem, a process and an outcome
quiz.why: People remember stories, and stories show your thinking.

quiz.question: What makes your thinking visible?
options: Showing decisions and the reasons and evidence behind them
quiz.why: Decisions show how you think.

quiz.question: Where should the summary go?
quiz.why: Busy readers should understand the project quickly.

quiz.question: What should the end of a case study include?
options: The outcome and what you learned
quiz.why: Reflection shows growth.

items.title: Write the story
items.description: Write like you're explaining it to a smart friend over chai. Short, specific and honest, with a point in every paragraph.

metadata.youllNeed: A text editor and a friend to read it.
metadata.practise: Publish your first case study (Stage 06 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Writing a case study: clear, specific and honest
metadata.seoDescription: Write your case study like you're explaining it to a smart friend. Learn to be specific, write headings that carry the point, and edit ruthlessly.

quiz.question: Which sentence is better for a case study?
options: I talked to five hostel students and noticed most screenshot their notes
quiz.why: It's specific, plain and true.

quiz.question: When should you use a number?
quiz.why: An invented number damages trust.

quiz.question: Which heading carries the point?
options: Students screenshot notes because they can't find them
quiz.why: Skimmers get the insight just from the heading.

quiz.question: Why include what you'd do differently?
quiz.why: Reflection reads as maturity.

items.title: Polish your visuals
items.description: Good visuals make your thinking easier to see. Use clear hierarchy, consistent spacing and a few strong images instead of every screen.

metadata.practise: Publish your first case study (Stage 06 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Polishing portfolio visuals: make your thinking easy to see
metadata.seoDescription: Good visuals make your thinking easier to follow. Learn how to choose images, keep things consistent, and show your work honestly.

quiz.question: What's the goal of polishing visuals?
options: Making your thinking easy to see
quiz.why: Presentation should help people notice your work, not replace it.

quiz.question: How many images should you aim for?
options: A focused set, around six to ten, that tells the story
quiz.why: Fewer, stronger images are easier to follow.

quiz.question: Which is dishonest?
options: Placing a screenshot in a fake app store listing to suggest it launched
quiz.why: It suggests something that isn't true.

quiz.question: What does the squint test show?
options: What stands out first on the page
quiz.why: It checks the hierarchy of your page.

items.title: Publish & share it
items.description: A link beats a PDF in a folder. Publish it somewhere people can open in one click, share it, and ask for real feedback.

metadata.practise: Publish your first case study (Stage 06 checkpoint).
metadata.seoTitle: Publishing and sharing your design portfolio
metadata.seoDescription: A link beats a PDF in a folder. Learn where to publish a case study, a checklist before you hit publish, and how to share it and ask for feedback.

quiz.question: Why publish a case study?
options: So people can actually see it, and so you can get feedback
quiz.why: Work that nobody can see can't help you grow.

quiz.question: Which is better as your main version?
options: A link people can open in one click
quiz.why: A link is easy to open and share. A PDF works well as an extra.

quiz.question: What should you check before publishing?
options: Links, phone view, typos, credits and private details
quiz.why: A quick check avoids easy mistakes.

quiz.question: How should you ask for feedback?
options: With a specific question, like "Was the problem clear on the first screen?"
quiz.why: Specific questions get useful answers.
